---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A finite set $X=\{x_1,\dots,x_N\}\subset \mathbb S^1$ is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $t$ if
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N p(x_j)=\int_{\mathbb S^1}p\,\,d\sigma
\]
for every restriction to $\mathbb S^1$ of a real polynomial in two variables of total degree at most $t$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:design}
For $X_N=\{e^{2\pi i j/N}:0\le j<N\}$,
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}q(\theta_j)
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}q(\theta)\,\,d\theta
\]
for every trigonometric polynomial
\[
 q(\theta)=\sum_{|k|\le N-1}c_k e^{ik\theta}.
\]
Consequently, $X_N$ is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $N-1$. This strength is sharp.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For an integer $k$,
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{ik\theta_j}
 =\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i kj/N}.
\]
The geometric sum equals $1$ when $N\mid k$ and $0$ otherwise. Hence it agrees with the circle integral for every $|k|\le N-1$. Linearity gives the quadrature formula. For sharpness, take the real function $q(\theta)=\cos(N\theta)$, the restriction of $\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)^N$. Its circle integral is zero while its discrete average is one, so the grid is not a design of strength $N$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
This is the finite exactness property of the periodic trapezoidal rule; see Trefethen and Weideman~\cite{Trefethen} for its convergence theory. It is also an equal-weight, or Chebyshev-type, quadrature rule for the low-frequency trigonometric space.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:cheb}
Let $M\ge1$ and define
\[
 \alpha_j=\frac{(2j-1)\pi}{2M},\qquad
 x_j=\cos\alpha_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,M.
\]
Then, for every algebraic polynomial $p$ of degree at most $2M-1$,
\[
 \frac1\pi\int_{-1}^1\frac{p(x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,\,d x
 =\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M p(x_j).
\]
Thus the $M$-point Gauss--Chebyshev rule is the even projection, under $x=\cos\theta$, of a half-step rotated $2M$-point equal-weight rule on $\mathbb S^1$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Consider the $2M$ equally spaced angles
\[
 \beta_j=\frac{(2j-1)\pi}{2M},\qquad j=1,\ldots,2M.
\]
They differ from the standard $2M$-point grid only by a rotation, so Theorem~\ref{thm:design} gives exactness for all trigonometric polynomials of degree at most $2M-1$. For $p$ of algebraic degree at most $2M-1$, the function $p(\cos\theta)$ is an even trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $2M-1$. Hence
\[
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}p(\cos\theta)\,\,d\theta
 =\frac1{2M}\sum_{j=1}^{2M}p(\cos\beta_j).
\]
The left side equals
\[
 \frac1\pi\int_0^\pi p(\cos\theta)\,\,d\theta
 =\frac1\pi\int_{-1}^1\frac{p(x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,\,d x.
\]
The $2M$ cosine values occur in pairs, so the right side reduces to $M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M p(x_j)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:polygon}
For $N\ge3$, the measure $\mu_N$ satisfies the Minkowski balance condition. The convex body $P_N$ with surface-area measure $S_{P_N}=\mu_N$ is, up to translation, the regular $N$-gon with side length
\[
 s_N=\frac{2\pi}{N}.
\]
We henceforth choose the representative whose center is the origin. Its circumradius and inradius are
\[
 R_N=\frac{\pi/N}{\sin(\pi/N)},
 \qquad
 r_N=\frac{\pi}{N}\cot\frac{\pi}{N}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The balance condition is
\[
 \int_{\mathbb S^1}u\,\,d\mu_N(u)
 =\frac{2\pi}{N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u_j=0,
\]
which follows from degree-one design exactness. By the discrete Minkowski theorem there is a polygon whose outward normals are the $u_j$ and whose side lengths are all $2\pi/N$, unique up to translation. In cyclic order the normal directions turn by the constant angle $2\pi/N$. Hence the edges have equal lengths and equal turning angles, so the polygon is regular. The radius formulas are the elementary relations
\[
 s_N=2R_N\sin\frac\pi N,
 \qquad
 r_N=R_N\cos\frac\pi N.
\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:mixedarea}
Let $N\ge3$. For every planar convex body $K$,
\[
 \boxed{\;V(P_N,K)-V(B^2,K)=\pi\,\mathcal E_N(h_K).\;}
\]
Consequently, if $h_K(\theta)$ is a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $N-1$, then
\[
 V(P_N,K)=V(B^2,K).
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By the mixed-area identity and the definitions of $S_{P_N}$ and $S_{B^2}$,
\[
 V(P_N,K)=\frac12\int h_K\,\,d S_{P_N}
 =\pi Q_Nh_K,
\]
whereas
\[
 V(B^2,K)=\frac12\int h_K\,\,d S_{B^2}
 =\pi Ih_K.
\]
Subtracting gives the formula. The exactness statement follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:design}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:hausdorff}
For every $N\ge3$ and the origin-centered polygon $P_N$,
\[
 \boxed{
 d_H(P_N,B^2)
 =1-\frac{\pi}{N}\cot\frac{\pi}{N}.}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 d_H(P_N,B^2)
 =\frac{\pi^2}{3N^2}+\frac{\pi^4}{45N^4}+O(N^{-6}).
\]
Since $X_N$ has design strength $t=N-1$,
\[
 d_H(P_N,B^2)=\frac{\pi^2}{3(t+1)^2}+O(t^{-4}).
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since $h_{B^2}\equiv1$,
\[
 d_H(P_N,B^2)=\max\{R_N-1,\,1-r_N\}.
\]
Put $x=\pi/N\in(0,\pi/3]$. To identify the larger term, observe that $1-r_N\ge R_N-1$ is equivalent to
\[
 2\ge x(\cot x+\csc x)=x\cot(x/2).
\]
Writing $y=x/2$, the elementary inequality $\tan y\ge y$ for $0\le y<\pi/2$ gives $y\cot y\le1$, hence $x\cot(x/2)\le2$. Therefore
\[
 d_H(P_N,B^2)=1-x\cot x.
\]
The Taylor expansion
\[
 x\cot x=1-\frac{x^2}{3}-\frac{x^4}{45}+O(x^6)
\]
gives the stated asymptotics.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:planar-stability}
For any two balanced, nondegenerate probability measures $\mu,\nu$ as above,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stability}
 \boxed{\quad d_H(K_\mu,K_\nu)\le\piW_1(\mu,\nu).\quad}
\end{equation}
With the stated perimeter and Steiner normalizations, the constant is independent of the number and sizes of atoms and of the concentration of the measures.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $\eta=\mu-\nu$ and $g=h_{K_\mu}-h_{K_\nu}$. The total mass and the first moments of $\eta$ vanish. Equation~\eqref{eq:green-distribution} shows that
\[
 \widetilde g(\theta)=2\pi\int_{\mathbb S^1}G(\theta-\phi)\,\,d\eta(\phi)
\]
satisfies $\widetilde g''+\widetilde g=2\pi\eta$: the cosine correction vanishes by balance. Its first harmonics vanish by~\eqref{eq:green-fourier}. The same equation and normalization hold for $g$. Their difference solves $v''+v=0$ with zero first harmonics, hence $g=\widetilde g$. Using~\eqref{eq:w1-definition} and~\eqref{eq:green-lip},
\[
 |g(\theta)|\le2\pi\operatorname{Lip}_{d_g}(G)W_1(\mu,\nu)=\piW_1(\mu,\nu).
\]
Taking the supremum proves~\eqref{eq:stability}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:w1}
For every $N\ge1$, with the geodesic metric,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:grid-w1}
 W_1(\nu_N,\sigma)=\frac\pi{2N}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Transport each arc Voronoi cell, of length $2\pi/N$ and $\sigma$-mass $1/N$, to its central node. Its cost summed over the grid is
\[
 \frac N{2\pi}\int_{-\pi/N}^{\pi/N}|\theta|\,\,d\theta=\frac\pi{2N}.
\]
This is a coupling with marginals $\sigma$ and $\nu_N$, proving the upper bound. Conversely, $f(u)=d_g(u,X_N)$ is $1$-Lipschitz, vanishes on $X_N$, and satisfies $\int f\,d\sigma=\pi/(2N)$. The dual formula~\eqref{eq:w1-definition} gives the matching lower bound.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:sharp-stability}
For $0<|a|<1$, let $d\mu_a=(1+a\cos2\theta)\,d\sigma$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-example}
 d_H(K_{\mu_a},B^2)=\frac{|a|}{3},\qquad
 W_1(\mu_a,\sigma)=\frac{|a|}{\pi}.
\end{equation}
In particular, no estimate $d_H(K_\mu,B^2)\le CW_1(\mu,\sigma)^\beta$ with $\beta>1$ and fixed $C$ holds uniformly near $\sigma$, even among smooth positive densities converging uniformly to $1$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The measure is positive and balanced. Its centered support function is
\[
 h_a(\theta)=1-\frac a3\cos2\theta,
 \qquad h_a''+h_a=1+a\cos2\theta>0.
\]
The positivity of $h_a''+h_a$ gives a smooth strictly convex body, and Minkowski uniqueness identifies it with $K_{\mu_a}$. This proves the Hausdorff formula. Every periodic $1$-Lipschitz function is absolutely continuous with $|f'|\le1$ almost everywhere. Integration by parts gives
\[
 \left|\int f\,d(\mu_a-\sigma)\right|
 =\left|-\frac a{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f'(\theta)\sin2\theta\,d\theta\right|
 \le\frac{|a|}{\pi}.
\]
Equality is attained by a periodic function with derivative
$f'(\theta)=-\operatorname{sgn}(a\sin2\theta)$ almost everywhere: this derivative has zero mean, so its primitive is periodic and $1$-Lipschitz for $d_g$. Duality proves the second identity. Thus $d_H=(\pi/3)W_1$ along this family as $a\to0$, which excludes every exponent $\beta>1$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:perturbation}
Let $N\ge3$ and let $\rho_N$ be a balanced probability measure not supported on an antipodal pair. If $\varepsilon_N=W_1(\rho_N,\nu_N)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:perturbation}
 \left|d_H(K_{\rho_N},B^2)-\left(1-\frac\pi N\cot\frac\pi N\right)\right|
 \le\pi\varepsilon_N.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\varepsilon_N=O(N^{-2})$ implies $d_H(K_{\rho_N},B^2)=O(N^{-2})$; if $\varepsilon_N=o(N^{-2})$, then
\[
 N^2d_H(K_{\rho_N},B^2)\longrightarrow\frac{\pi^2}{3}.
\]
If $\rho_N=N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\delta_{\widetilde u_j}$ satisfies the stated assumptions, matching each perturbed node to its original node gives
$\varepsilon_N\le N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}d_g(\widetilde u_j,u_j)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The reverse triangle inequality for Hausdorff distance and~\eqref{eq:stability} give
\[
 |d_H(K_{\rho_N},B^2)-d_H(P_N,B^2)|
 \le d_H(K_{\rho_N},P_N)\le\pi\varepsilon_N.
\]
Use Theorem~\ref{thm:hausdorff}. The node estimate follows from the coupling that matches each perturbed node to its original node.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
